entry.title: 6 of 40 sites were pointing Google at a sitemap URL that returns HTML
entry.summary:
A robots.txt Sitemap line that resolves to 200 is not the same thing as a readable sitemap. I found out the expensive way, on six sites at once, and the bug had been live for months. $ curl -sI https://example.com/sitemap.xml.gz HTTP/2 200 content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8
That is the entire bug, and it is completely invisible to normal monitoring. The chain is boring and extremely common: The site was originally built with a generator that gzipped its sitemap, so robots.txt got Sitemap: https://example.com/sitemap.xml.gz. The build changed (Hugo out, a SPA build in). The .gz file stopped being produced. The web server has the standard single-page-app fallback:
location / { try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html; }

entry.title: Caching Is Easy. Cache Invalidation Is Where Systems Break: A Practical Guide
entry.summary:
Adding a cache takes ten minutes. Debugging the bug it causes six months later takes a week. Caching trades correctness for speed. The senior move is deciding how much correctness you're willing to give up, and making that decision explicit. Before you reach for Redis, answer three things: How stale can this data be? (seconds, minutes, never) What does a wrong answer cost? (a flicker, or a wrong invoice) What's the read-to-write ratio? (caches pay off on read-heavy data) If you can't answer #1, you're not ready to cache it. entry.title: Why I Practice Coding Interviews Out Loud
entry.summary: For a long time I prepared for coding interviews by solving problems silently. I could solve medium problems on my own, then froze in real interviews. The problem was not the algorithms. It was talking while thinking. In a live coding round, the interviewer is grading your communication as much as your code. They want to hear you clarify the problem, propose a brute-force approach, explain why it is slow and then improve it. If you have never practised narrating, the first time you do it is under pressure. Read the problem aloud and restate it in my own words. Ask two clarifying questions, even if I think I know the answer (input size, edge cases, duplicates). Say the brute force first and its complexity. Talk through the optimisation before writing a line of code. Code while narrating what each block does. Test with one normal case and one edge case out loud. I set a 35-minute timer for each problem. After each run I review what I actually said. I started using ClapAssist for this, since it has a coding mode and gives a recap of the session, but a simple screen recording works too. The goal is to catch habits like going silent for two minutes or skipping complexity analysis. Within three weeks my mock interview feedback shifted from "good solution, hard to follow" to "clear communicator." Same algorithms, very different result. If you are grinding problems but struggling in real rounds, try practising out loud for a week. It is uncomfortable at first and then it becomes your biggest advantage.

entry.title: How to Run a Brainstorming Session That Actually Works
entry.summary: In 1953, advertising executive Alex Osborn promised that a group brainstorming together could think up twice as many ideas as the same people working alone. In 1958, Taylor, Berry and Block at Yale ran 12 real groups of four through three problems using Osborn's official rules: no criticism, freewheeling, quantity first, build on each other's ideas. entry.title: Dirty flash vs clean flash: when your Galaxy actually needs a full wipe
entry.summary: When people talk about flashing Samsung firmware with Odin, one question comes up in almost every thread: "Do I need to wipe my phone first?" The answer most people give — always wipe — is wrong as often as it's right. There's a real distinction between a dirty flash and a clean flash, and knowing which one your situation needs saves you from both data loss and pointless re-setup. A "dirty flash" is flashing new firmware over your existing installation without wiping user data — the phone keeps your apps, settings, and files, and the new system replaces the old one underneath. A "clean flash" wipes everything (the data partition) and starts the phone from a blank state, like it just came out of the box.
